series.name: Employment Situation (Jobs Report)
series.releasePattern: First Friday of each month, 8:30am ET
series.topicLine: The headline US jobs report — nonfarm payrolls and unemployment rate.
series.whatItMeasures: Net change in nonfarm payroll employment and the unemployment rate, from two Census-run surveys (~119K businesses and ~60K households). Broken out by industry, age, race, and education.
series.whyItMatters: The single most-cited labor market signal. AI's aggregate effect (or lack thereof) shows up here first if it's happening at scale. Prior-month revisions often reveal that early estimates over- or under-stated the trend.

lastIngested.value: +165K nonfarm vs a +48K 12-month average; U-rate 4.1%; August revised +133K to +186K and September +29K to +60K, 84K higher combined; professional and business services +70K and +269K since its Oct 2025 low

series.nextExpected: December 4, 2026 (November data), 8:30am ET
series.sweepNote: Swept 2026-11-09: ingested the October report, published Nov 6. Three overlays on overall-us-displacement, white-collar-professional-displacement and financial-services-displacement; payroll counts are not a '% of jobs displaced' or '% of roles displaced', so overlays rather than data points - the same unit call as every prior Employment Situation ingest, not caution. The release runs against the displacement thesis in both of the lines that matter: nonfarm +165K against a +48K prior-12-month average, and professional and business services +70K, now +269K since a recent low in October 2025. Information was -1K and financial activities +7K, both inside the 'little change' list. The revisions also flipped sign from last month - August to +186K and September to +60K, 84K higher combined, where the September release had cut July and August by 60K. July 2026 has now been published with three different trend signs across vintages, so weight any first print lightly until both its revisions are in. bls.gov serves 403 to automated fetchers; the archived release at https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/empsit_11062026.htm reads fine through a renderer, and the bls.gov/schedule pages answer a plain fetch.

series.name: BLS Employment Projections (incl. AI exposure categories)
series.cadenceLabel: Annual projections round, typically late summer
series.releasePattern: Ten-year projections published annually; the 2025-35 round landed August 2026. AI-specific products appear under /emp/publications/ and Table 1.12 'Factors affecting occupational utilization' is refreshed each cycle.
series.topicLine: The only official US government occupational AI exposure classification, plus the ten-year occupational projections it complements.
series.whatItMeasures: Ten-year industry and occupational employment projections, and since the 2025-35 round a four-category relative AI exposure classification (Low/Moderate/High/Very high) covering 831 detailed occupations, built by combining five external exposure measures on a 2018 SOC basis. Published with a downloadable XLSX pairing categories to projections.
series.whyItMatters: Every other exposure estimate on the site is academic or think-tank modeling. This is the federal statistical agency's own classification, and it explicitly supersedes three inputs already ingested individually (Eloundou, Eisfeldt, Felten) for any aggregate exposure claim. It is also SOC-coded, so it joins directly onto the 342-occupation scorecard.

lastIngested.value: Four relative AI exposure categories across 831 occupations; 211 of 4,155 source-occupation cells imputed, affecting 75 occupations

series.nextExpected: 2027 (2026-36 projections round, per BLS)
series.sweepNote: Added 2026-08-28 after the AI exposure categories page (last modified 2026-08-27) was found via user tip rather than by sweep — BLS Employment Projections was not on this registry, so nothing flagged it. BLS hard-blocks all automated retrieval (403 with an explicit anti-bot notice on both WebFetch and curl, including the XLSX), so this series must be swept manually or via a browser; do not expect an adapter to work.

series.name: Challenger Job Cuts Report (with AI attribution)
series.releasePattern: First Thursday of each month
series.topicLine: Employer-announced layoffs with a specific 'AI-attributed' category.
series.whatItMeasures: Job-cut announcements tracked from public sources, self-reported employer rationale, and Challenger's outreach. Uniquely tags cuts where AI is named as the driver.
series.whyItMatters: The most-cited source when the media reports 'AI-driven layoffs.' Signal is early but noisy — attribution reflects what employers say publicly, which may over- or under-state AI's actual role.

lastIngested.value: 121,401 AI-attributed cuts YTD (20% of all 617,189 cuts); AI cited in only 1,265 October cuts, its lowest month of 2026, and Market/Economic Conditions (130,531 YTD) has overtaken AI as the leading 2026 reason

series.nextExpected: December 3, 2026 (November data)
series.sweepNote: Swept 2026-11-09: ingested the October report, published Nov 5. The headline is the attribution reversal, not the totals: AI was cited for just 1,265 October cuts, its lowest monthly total of the year, and 'with 130,531 cuts so far this year, Market/Economic Conditions has overtaken Artificial Intelligence (AI) as the leading reason for job cuts in 2026.' AI had led every prior month of 2026 and now sits second at 121,401 YTD, about 20% of all cuts. Three overlays on overall-us-displacement and one on tech-sector-displacement (Technology 5,576 October cuts, its lowest month of the year, but still 171,501 YTD and 28% of all 2026 cuts, already past its full-year 2025 total). October cuts 43,994, the lowest October since 2023 and -71% year over year; 617,189 YTD, -44%. Two cautions worth carrying forward: the two leading reasons are only 9,130 cuts apart, so the ranking could flip back next month, and Challenger attribution reflects what employers say publicly, so this is at least as much a change in corporate framing as in cause - Challenger says as much ('the reasons employers give have shifted from technology to the economy'). Also note the hiring figure flatters: Amazon's 300,000 seasonal hires account for nearly all of Technology's 300,252 announced hires.

series.whyItMatters: Fills the gap between quarterly earnings and monthly BLS — private data with a real-time cadence. Ramp's finding that AI-intensive firms are adding jobs faster than laggards is a key counter to the displacement narrative.

series.name: Census Business Trends & Outlook Survey — AI Supplement
series.releasePattern: Alternating Thursdays
series.topicLine: The freshest firm-side AI adoption measure available in the US.
series.whatItMeasures: The share of ~1.2M US businesses that report using AI in the past two weeks. Broken out by sector, state, and the 25 largest MSAs. Question wording revised in Nov 2025 to include 'any business function' (up from the narrower 'production of goods and services' framing), roughly doubling the measured rate.
series.whyItMatters: Highest-frequency US firm-level adoption signal. Because it's biweekly, it reveals turn-of-quarter shifts that quarterly surveys miss. Adoption still concentrated in Information (49.6%) and Finance and Insurance (42.7%), both at cycle highs.

lastIngested.value: 25.0% national AI use (SE 0.60%), two weeks ending Nov 1 2026 (cycle 202623); series high and its first reading at or above 25%, up 0.8pp from cycle 202622's 24.2%, which is about one standard error of the difference. Q28 six-month expectation 28.2%. Second reading of the three AI follow-ups: employee generative-SI use 27.6%, effect on headcount 7.3% up / 2.4% down, on new hires 2.3% up / 3.0% down - the Q9/Q10 sign asymmetry repeats. Sector: Information 49.6%, Educational Services 44.0%, Finance and Insurance 42.7%.

series.nextExpected: Biweekly, roughly every two weeks; cycle 202624 publishes around Dec 3, 2026 (reference period ending Nov 15; collection runs Nov 16 to Nov 29 per the "Collection and Reference Dates" sheet). The AI questions run in EVERY cycle - an earlier note here claiming the July 30, 2026 wave carried no AI content was wrong, inferred from the press releases, which are boilerplate and never mention AI. Always read https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/downloads/National.xlsx (and Sector.xlsx) rather than the release text. Date each value to its reference-period end (see the 'Collection and Reference Dates' sheet), not the publication date - they differ by six to seven weeks. The Nov 17, 2025 rewording from AI use “in producing goods or services” to “in any business function”, and the Oct 22, 2026 relabel of AI as “Super Intelligence or SI”, are both same-construct instrument changes; Census and we both publish one continuous series. QUESTION NUMBERS MOVE - read them from the workbook, never from a prior note. As of cycle 202622, current use is Q7 and the six-month expectation is Q28, not Q24 (Q24 is now the inventories question; the cycle 202621 note here recorded the expectation as Q24 and that number is now wrong). Cycle 202622 is the first to carry the three core AI questions from FR Doc. 2026-18304: Q8 employee generative-SI use, Q9 AI's effect on total headcount over six months, Q10 AI's effect on new hires. All three run behind skip logic and are asked ONLY of businesses answering yes to Q7, so their denominator is AI-using firms, not all firms - check this before reading any of them as an economy-wide share. They are firm counts, not job counts, so they are overlays on the displacement charts, not data points. The biannual AI Supplement is a separate instrument with an 11-week reference window - do not let its release date make it the latest point.
series.sweepNote: Swept 2026-11-23: ingested cycle 202623 (published Nov 19), 25.0% (SE 0.60%) for the reference period ending 2026-11-01. This is the series high and its first reading at or above 25%, but the 0.8pp rise over cycle 202622's 24.2% is about one standard error of the difference, so read it as a new high rather than as acceleration; ai-adoption-rate uses aggregationMethod "latest", so currentValue moves 24.2 -> 25.0 on this one point, confirmed against computeAggregate. The open question from the last sweep is now answered: the response-quality shift did NOT revert. 'Do not know' on Q7 is 13.3% against 13.9% and 9.6% in the two prior cycles, and the standard error on the yes share is 0.60% against 0.61% and 0.27%. Two consecutive cycles at the new level means this is a level shift that arrived with the three new follow-up questions, not noise - so cycle-to-cycle comparisons from 202622 onward are sound, but standard errors from 202621 and earlier are not comparable with them. Treat that as the standing read rather than re-opening it each cycle. Q8/Q9/Q10 now have a prior reading: Q8 27.6% from 26.8%, Q9 7.3% up / 2.4% down from 6.6% / 2.5%, Q10 2.3% up / 3.0% down from 2.5% / 3.3%. The Q9-versus-Q10 sign asymmetry repeats, which is the substantive finding of this cycle - on existing headcount AI-using firms report gains over losses about three to one, on new hiring slightly more report a fall than a rise. Still overlays, still for the denominator reason: skip logic asks these only of firms answering yes to Q7, so they describe AI-using firms and count firms rather than jobs. Also updated whyItMatters, whose sector figures were four months stale: Information is now 49.6% (was quoted at 39.7%) and Finance and Insurance 42.7% (was 33.9%). Read sector values from Sector.xlsx, same URL pattern as National.xlsx. Fixed the stale BTOS figure quoted in ai-adoption-rate's disclaimer prose, 23.8% -> 25.0%; it had been carried through at least three sweeps.

series.name: GenAI Adoption Tracker / FRED RPS GenAI series (Bick, Blandin, Deming)
series.publisher: St. Louis Fed / Harvard (Real-Time Population Survey)
series.releasePattern: Roughly every 3 months at genaiadoptiontracker.com; since Jul 24, 2026 also published as 137 official FRED series (category 8), updated quarterly
series.topicLine: The definitive quarterly measure of US worker generative AI adoption — now official FRED data.
series.whatItMeasures: Share of US adults 18-64 using generative AI (a) overall and (b) at work, fielded quarterly via the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS) since August 2024. The FRED release (137 series, added Jul 2026) adds machine-readable vintages for usage rates (overall/work/nonwork), time savings, GenAI-assisted work hours, and PC/internet adoption comparisons, with industry and occupation breakdowns. Key series: RPSGENAIUSAGESHAREWORK, RPSGENAIUSAGESHAREALL, RPSGENAITSALL, RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL.
series.whyItMatters: The single cleanest time series on worker-side GenAI adoption in the US, cited by every major synthesis (Stanford DEL, IMF, Fed, OECD). Nationally representative and cadence-consistent. FRED hosting makes it citable and API-accessible alongside official government statistics.

lastIngested.value: Q3 2026 wave (fielded Aug 2026): work adoption 40.5%, down 4.65 points from 45.2% in Q2; overall 60.8%; assisted work hours 5.3%

series.nextExpected: ~January 2026 for the Q4 2026 wave; FRED updated the Q3 series on Oct 20, 2026, roughly 11 weeks after the Q2 update. Read the four key series straight off FRED without a key: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=RPSGENAIUSAGESHAREWORK (also RPSGENAIUSAGESHAREALL, RPSGENAITSALL, RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL). FRED dates each observation to the quarter start; the authors' tracker labels the same wave by field month, and the chart dates points to the field month (FRED quarter start plus one month). Check genaiadoptiontracker.com for the headline wording, and expect FRED to revise the prior quarter.

series.name: Yale Budget Lab — Tracking AI's Impact on the Labor Market
series.releasePattern: Each new CPS release; typically monthly commentary, quarterly deep-dives
series.topicLine: The main counter-evidence to the ADP 'Canaries' finding — no aggregate AI-labor effect visible in CPS.
series.whatItMeasures: Uses the Current Population Survey to test whether AI-exposed occupations are seeing employment declines. Complements the ADP-based Canaries with a different dataset and a different unit of analysis.
series.whyItMatters: The Yale team's 'no effect yet' reading disciplines the field — anyone claiming AI-driven displacement has to reconcile with CPS data that doesn't show it. Their published disagreements with Stanford DEL are among the most important debates in the field.

lastIngested.value: Tracker extended to August 2026 CPS; still no clear AI labor-market disruption

series.name: Stanford DEL — AI Economic Indicators (Canaries + Takeoff + Adoption)
series.releasePattern: Research notes ~quarterly; dashboards update monthly at digitaleconomy.stanford.edu
series.topicLine: Three linked dashboards: employment by age × AI exposure, macro takeoff signals, and worker adoption.
series.whatItMeasures: Canaries Dashboard tracks employment across 5-year balanced ADP payroll sample (25K firms, 4.6M workers). Takeoff Tracker follows 12 macro indicators for AI-driven growth. Adoption Monitor synthesizes surveys.
series.whyItMatters: The Canaries finding — early-career workers 22-25 in most-exposed occupations now at -4.2% year over year as of October 2026 data, below their year-earlier level every month since October 2023 — is the most-cited AI-displacement evidence in the field. The Transformation Tracker, renamed from the Takeoff Tracker, reads 3 of 12 macro indicators clearly above pre-2020 trend, all of them capital measures, and is the field's best macro summary.
